segments.text: As we come down from the Rocca, we return to the streets of the town.
And this time, I suggest you look up.
In front of you is the Torre dell'Orologio, the Clock Tower.
From a distance, it's my Rocca that dominates Vicopisano.
But walking through these streets, especially along Via Lante, it's hard not to notice this tower.
Tall, narrow…
and decidedly distinctive.
And before you ask:
no, I didn't build this one either.
Its original structure dates from the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, so it was already here long before I arrived.
It was probably built as a military tower, to watch over the road leading to the old stronghold, around Palazzo Pretorio.
Look at it carefully.
It's built almost entirely of verrucano.
And along its walls you can still see a series of large stone corbels.
In the Middle Ages, they supported projecting wooden structures, reached through those small arched doorways you can still see today.
On a tower built for military purposes, spaces projecting outwards also made it easier to watch over and defend the area at the foot of the walls.
But then the tower ceased to serve a defensive purpose.
And rather than pull it down…
they transformed it.
Its height made it ideal for a new task:
becoming a bell tower.
And, a few centuries later, the clock arrived too.
It's documented here from at least the sixteenth century, while the mechanism that survives today dates from the eighteenth.
A military tower.
Then a bell tower.
Then a clock.
I have to say, I approve.
A good building doesn't necessarily have to do the job it was built for forever.
It needs to go on serving the people around it.
Today, following major restoration work, the tower is open to visitors. You can climb to the bell chamber, with views over Vicopisano and Monte Pisano.
But perhaps what intrigues me most is something else.
A structure built to watch people passing by…
is now used mainly to mark the passing of time.
Not a bad transformation.
Now let's continue downhill.
Our next stop will take us to the Pieve di Santa Maria, the parish church.
There, at least for a few minutes, we'll leave towers, walls and fortifications behind.
